content.p: On 1 April 1941, in a forest clearing called Varnița near Fântâna Albă, Soviet border troops opened machine-gun fire on a column of Romanian-speaking villagers who were walking, with icons and a white flag, towards the frontier with Romania. They had been told, or had heard, that the border would be opened for them. Historians in Romania describe the rumour as a trap laid by the Soviet security service, the NKVD.

Nobody knows how many people died. Estimates run from a few dozen, in Soviet-era figures, to about 3,000 in Romanian commemorations, and the argument over the number has continued for eight decades. The Romanian and Moldovan sources describe the marchers as unarmed civilians from the Siret valley who were fired on by border guards, and say that many participants were arrested or deported afterwards. A Soviet-era statement from 1991 told it differently, claiming that the crowd opened fire first. For decades the event could not be discussed openly on either side of the border.

In June 1940 Romania accepted a Soviet ultimatum and gave up a territory of more than three million inhabitants, including northern Bukovina and Bessarabia. Once the Romanian administration and army had withdrawn, the Red Army and the NKVD moved in. According to the Adevărul account, many families were caught off guard by the speed of events and found relatives on both sides of the new frontier. Many tried to rejoin them, legally if possible and illegally if not.

Historia, citing official Soviet reports, says that 471 people crossed illegally from the Hliboca, Herța, Putila and Storojineț areas, and that official Ukrainian data showed more than 7,000 people had fled to Romania after the first year of occupation. Historian Constantin Ungureanu gives a figure of 3,218 people who left 23 villages of Herța county alone. The authorities drew up lists of families with relatives across the border, declared them "traitors" and deported them to forced labour in Siberia and Kazakhstan. The same article says that lists of the patrol unit held about 1,085 names on 1 January 1941 and that another list from 7 December 1940 held 1,294.

The first violent crossings came before April. On the night of 15 or 19 November 1940 (Historia gives the 15th, Ungureanu the 19th), about 40 families from Suceveni, 105 people in all, forced the border near Fântâna Albă. Three of them were killed in a clash with the patrols and two wounded people were captured; the rest reached Romania. Their relatives were deported. In the night of 6 to 7 February 1941, a group of several hundred people from Mahala and other villages near Chernivtsi, about 400 according to Ungureanu and 500 according to Historia, tried to cross near Lunca and were fired on by Soviet border guards. Only 57 reached Romania. Historia adds that 44 people were arrested and that 12 of them were later sentenced to death.
content.h2: The rumour of an open border
content.p: Ungureanu describes a brief thaw in Romanian-Soviet relations in February 1941, which allowed a repatriation commission in Chernivtsi (Cernăuți) to resume work on 15 February. In early spring a rumour spread that residents had been given the right to leave. Romanians of the Siret valley crowded into the offices of the Hliboca district with applications to be repatriated, hoping, he writes, to receive the same right that ethnic Germans of northern Bukovina had been given in autumn 1940.

Ungureanu concludes that no official decision on repatriating Romanians had been taken, and that Soviet officials and provocateurs spread the rumour to learn how the local population felt about Soviet power and to identify people disloyal to it. The author of a HotNews commentary reaches a similar conclusion. In that reading, Soviet security files from the winter of 1940-41 spoke of "cleansing" the Ukrainian republic of anti-Soviet elements, and the NKVD encouraged lists of would-be emigrants while it repeatedly hinted at an imminent opening of the border. The commentary argues that the deliberate delay in delivering on the supposed promise provoked the mass attempts at Lunca and at Varnița. Because the villagers spoke neither Russian nor Ukrainian, according to Ungureanu, village council representatives filled in the applications for them.

On 26 March 1941 crowds gathered in Storojineț to submit applications. Ungureanu reports that Vasile Luca, a Romanian communist who had settled in the USSR and had been elected to the Supreme Soviet of the Ukrainian republic, addressed them, telling them that spies and saboteurs had put the idea of leaving into their heads and asking whether they wanted to work for landowners and the bourgeoisie. The speech, he says, angered the crowd further.

On 1 April a large group from villages in the Siret valley set out for the border. Ungureanu estimates the column at about 2,000 people. Historia and the Romanian embassy in Ukraine speak of more than 3,000. The marchers carried a white flag and religious emblems: icons, banners and crosses made of fir branches. A pursuing group of mounted soldiers followed them at a distance of one to one and a half kilometres after they left Hliboca, Ungureanu writes. He says the column turned back towards Suceveni, then covered about eight or nine kilometres of forest track and reached Fântâna Albă, where border guards tried to stop it and the villagers kept going.

Towards evening the column reached Varnița, a clearing about two kilometres from the frontier by Ungureanu's account (Historia and News Bucovina say about three). Ungureanu says freshly dug trenches ran along three sides of the clearing, held by armed border guards and soldiers. When the front of the column was about 100 metres from the soldiers, a Soviet officer ordered the crowd to halt. Those in front stopped, but the people behind pushed forward, and the machine guns opened fire from several directions. The Digi24 report quotes Radu Bruja, a historian at the Ștefan cel Mare University in Suceava, who says the marchers were flanked by border units with cavalry behind them. The same report quotes the Chernivtsi journalist Ștefan Broască, who says an old man with a white beard was carried at the front so that the march would be seen as peaceful.

Survivors gave their own accounts. Gheorghe Sidoreac, aged 17 at the time and interviewed by Digi24 when he was one of the last survivors, said the agitators had shouted that people should raise their hands and show handkerchiefs and would not be shot, and that the machine guns then fired low. He said he fell and saw an officer with a revolver shooting the wounded, and that he later found piles of bodies several metres high. Gheorghe Mihailiuc, a teacher quoted in Adevărul, recalled that the guns waited until the crowd had come out into the clearing, that someone shouted "Down!" and that a young man holding a tricolour fell shouting that he would die for freedom. Another survivor, Gheorghe Isopescu of Suceveni, recalled that an older villager, Hariton Amari, had urged the crowd to avoid Fântâna Albă because guards would be waiting there, but that the column ignored him, according to Ungureanu.

What happened to the wounded is told more vaguely. Historia, drawing on documents of the period and local testimony, says the survivors were chased by cavalry and cut down with sabres, that the wounded were dragged by horses to five mass graves dug in advance, and that some were buried alive. The same article says that other captured villagers were taken to Hliboca, tortured by the NKVD and thrown into a mass grave in the Jewish cemetery there. The account of the pits and the burials alive rests on witness statements and on documents Historia does not identify, and it should be read as uncorroborated. Adevărul, News Bucovina and Radio Moldova repeat that the wounded were killed or buried alive, but only as what local witnesses said or as a bare assertion, and none names a document. The figure of five graves and the cemetery grave appear only in Historia, while Ungureanu says only that some of those shot were buried in several mass graves near the forest.
The number is the central dispute, and it should be read as a range with a name attached to each estimate.

Ungureanu, writing in a Moldovan academic journal, says that no one knows how many were shot and that about 200 is the estimate. Căruntu says that KGB documents speak of only 20 dead, which he calls far from reality, and that the toll has been exaggerated to 7,000 or even 15,000. He accepts the figures of a document of the Romanian Special Intelligence Service that he found in the national archives in Bucharest, which records 200 dead and 500 wounded, to which he adds the hundreds who were convicted and deported afterwards.

Romanian media and officials use larger numbers. Digi24 and the Romanian embassy in Ukraine speak of nearly or more than 3,000 killed; Radio Moldova of between 2,000 and 4,000; Historia of between 2,000 and 3,000 in its description of the march, while its headline says "over 2,000". Ion Varta, a professor from Chișinău, said that estimates by various authors run between 1,400 and 2,400. The HotNews commentary says that scientific documentation, hindered by the deliberate concealment of archive files, has established only a few dozen names for the Lunca and Varnița events together. Ungureanu lists the dead identified by incomplete information as 16 from Pătrăuți de Jos, 12 from Dimca, 7 from Carapciu, 5 from Cupca, 5 from Suceveni and 3 from Pătrăuți de Sus.

The low end of the range comes from the Soviet period. Veridica quotes the 2 April 1991 issue of the newspaper Timp nou, in which the Communist Party stated that the crowd had opened fire first, that the army returned fire and that 24 people were killed and 43 wounded. Ungureanu separately records that around 19:00 on 1 April a group of 100 to 120 people from Carapciu, Iordănești and Prisăcăreni was attacked at the edge of Suceveni, with 24 dead and 43 wounded. The sources do not say whether the Soviet-era statement and this report describe the same event.

The shooting was followed by repression. Ungureanu reports that many participants and their families were arrested and deported to Siberia or Kazakhstan, and that 22 people were charged with instigating the march. One, Vasile Grijincu, was sentenced to death and his wife and eight children were deported to Kazakhstan. Sixteen were given ten years of forced labour by a military tribunal, and five more received eight years. Of the 22 convicted, 19 died in the camps; three, Ilie Vasca, Teodor Dâca and Orest Dugan, returned home in 1961.

In the night of 12 to 13 June 1941, Soviet troops rounded up more than 13,000 Romanians and deported them to Siberia and Kazakhstan, according to Historia. Ungureanu gives different figures for the Chernivtsi region: 2,279 families with 7,720 people deported on 13 June, and, from another estimate, 22,147 people of several nationalities, of whom 6,036 (27.2 percent) were Romanian. He notes that it is unclear whether the second figure covers 13 June only or all of 1941. Romanian officials link these deportations to the march, since many of those deported were relatives of the dead.
content.h2: Silence, denial and a disputed memory
content.p: The Soviet authorities never acknowledged the massacre, Radio Moldova reports, and it came to light only in the perestroika years and after the collapse of the USSR, when archives opened. Mircea Druc, a former prime minister of Moldova, told Digi24 that until 1990 families spoke of it only in code, saying in oblique terms that an uncle had died at Fântâna Albă. Romania's minister-delegate for Romanians abroad, Dan Stoenescu, said at the 75th anniversary in 2016 that it had been unmentionable on both sides of the border for more than half a century.

Soviet accounts presented the event as the work of foreign intelligence. Veridica, summarising such narratives, says the Communist Party announcement of 1991 blamed rumours spread by agents of "Fascist Germany and monarchist Romania". Its authors argue that this account sought both to obscure details and to remove blame from the Soviet regime.

The dispute resurfaced on the eve of the 80th anniversary in 2021. The Chernivtsi Regional State Administration posted a video on Facebook which, according to News Bucovina, described the killings as a provocation consciously planned by Romanian secret services against the people of Bukovina (the wording is translated here) and put the number shot at about 50 people, without saying that they were ethnic Romanians. The Romanian embassy in Ukraine said that historical truth must be respected in any portrayal of the massacre, and described the victims as more than 3,000 peasants encircled and killed by NKVD troops. Veridica calls the video a carry-over of Soviet narrative and notes that the National Council of Romanians in Ukraine asked the governor of Chernivtsi to dismiss the claims. HotNews adds that the word "Romanian" was later removed from several of the administration's materials.

A round table held at the Chernivtsi national university on 30 March 2018, reported by the historian Marin Gherman, showed how far apart interpretations can be. Ukrainian and Romanian historians took different positions. Some Ukrainian participants argued that the 1941 killings were a consequence of Romania's 1918 union with Bukovina, which they called a "Romanian occupation" that turned into "a boomerang". Romanian historians from both countries criticised that thesis as unprovable and urged researchers to avoid manipulation of this kind. Gherman also noted that the Ukrainian press often ignores that the victims were ethnic Romanians and uses the general term "Bukovinians".

Ukrainian authorities first allowed a religious service for the victims at Fântâna Albă in 2000, according to Radio Moldova. Gherman records that King Michael I of Romania visited the place during a trip to northern Bukovina on 30 May 1999, where priests held a memorial service. Digi24 reported in 2013 that a wooden cross raised in 2003 was the only marker of the tragedy there. Romania's Chamber of Deputies adopted on 12 April 2011 the bill that made 1 April a national day honouring Romanians who were victims of the massacres at Fântâna Albă and other places, and of deportations, famine and other repression by the Soviet regime in Herța, northern Bukovina and Bessarabia.

Services continue each year. In 2017 several hundred people in mourning dress or folk costume gathered at the site, according to Radio Free Europe. In 2024, priests led by Archimandrite Melchisedec Velnic, abbot of Putna Monastery in Romania, held a memorial service at Putna for the "over 2,000" Romanians killed, and Velnic proposed building an Orthodox hermitage on the land of the massacre. Some Romanian historians and commentators compare Fântâna Albă to the Katyn massacre; Radu Bruja told Digi24 that nobody has taken responsibility for the crime and that this crime belongs to the same chain of Soviet crimes against the peoples of Central Europe. Digi24 added that the massacre is not talked about in school history lessons, and Radio Moldova wrote that the Soviet regime never acknowledged it.
